title: Line Following: Building the Behaviour
description: Two sensors, four possible readings, four decisions. Build the rule table yourself and watch it actually drive.

content.value: One IR sensor can only tell you what's directly underneath it. Put two side by side, straddling a line, and something more useful becomes possible: the pattern of which sensor sees the line tells you which way the robot has drifted, and that's enough information to steer back.

L   R
   [ IR ] [ IR ]      <- two sensors, straddling the line
      \\   //
       \\ //
     ----X----          <- the dark line

With two sensors, there are exactly four possible combinations of readings. Each one tells you something specific about where the robot is relative to the line — and each needs its own response to correct course.

content.title: 〰️ Build the table, then test it
content.hint: Think it through before testing: if only the left sensor sees the line, which way has the robot drifted, and which way should it turn to get back on?

content.value: Notice what happens with a wrong rule in that last row especially: get "both sensors off the line" backwards and the robot doesn't just fail quietly — it visibly overcorrects, oscillates, or drives straight off the track. This is a real closed-loop control problem, the same shape you'll meet again and again in robotics: sense, decide, correct, repeat, many times a second.

Nobody is steering this robot — it's reacting entirely to what its own sensors tell it, moment to moment. That's the sense-think-act loop from Module 1, running for real, many times a second, with hardware you now understand every part of.

Real line followers often use more than two sensors (five or seven is common) for smoother, more graduated correction instead of a hard left/right snap. The two-sensor version you just built is the same idea, simplified to its essentials.

Key takeaway: two IR sensors straddling a line give four possible readings, and a rule table mapping each one to a response — forward, left, right, stop — is enough to build a real line-following behaviour.

quiz.question: Only the left sensor sees the line; the right sensor sees the floor. Which way has the robot drifted, and what should it do?
options: It's drifted right of the line — turn left to recentre
It's drifted left of the line — turn right to recentre
quiz.explain: If the line has moved under the left sensor, the robot itself has drifted to the right relative to it — turning left brings it back.

quiz.question: What happens in the widget's simulation if the 'both sensors off the line' rule is set incorrectly?
options: Nothing changes, that row doesn't matter
The robot can oscillate or drive straight off the track when it loses the line entirely
The simulation ignores incorrect rules automatically
quiz.explain: That row handles the case where the robot has lost the line completely — get it wrong and there's no way to recover once it happens.

quiz.question: Why is line following described as the sense-think-act loop from Module 1, 'running for real'?
options: Because someone is remote-controlling it the whole time
Because the robot senses its sensors, decides an action from the rule table, and acts, continuously, without a human deciding each move
It isn't really the same loop, just a coincidence in naming
quiz.explain: Every element — sensing, deciding, acting, repeating — is present and running on real hardware-shaped logic, exactly the loop Module 1 introduced as an idea.
